questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Personal connection to the destination (heritage / friends there/ etc.)

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: There were multiple reasons for choosing Erasmus Universiteit as the destination. Academically, Erasmus Universiteit is a well-renowned university that offers an international environment with high-quality finance courses, which is what I was after. Secondly, having a Dutch father I am closely connected to Dutch culture from my childhood, but I wanted to explore it on my own by living and studying in the Netherlands. Finally, not only Erasmus Universiteit but Rotterdam itself has a huge and vibrant international environment.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I enjoyed my semester abroad in Rotterdam and would recommend it to others.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: It was extremely easy. First and foremost because Erasmus School of Economics has an amazing coordinator who is extremely helpful and provides all necessary information. Moreover, everyone speaks English and many websites can be found in English, so searching for information online is easy.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: The exchange coordinator helped me register for courses.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: As mentioned, the coordinator invites you to a Facebook group and makes daily updates. Moreover, she sends on-going mails to you with the important deadlines and information and she is fairly quick to answer.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: Fairly difficult due to the shortage of housing all over Europe in big cities. The struggle is present in Rotterdam as well and I was admitted to the Erasmus Programme late.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: I can recommend it. Most people try to find housing in Kralingen, which is located in between the city centre and campus. However, this is also where demand is highest. City centre is the second most demanded place to live in the city. On-campus you will live with other exchange students and people seemed to enjoy it. This is also where a lot of international student parties will be hosted. People seemed to be in larger groups and do more activities together when they lived on-campus as they spent more time with other internationals. Housing in Kralingen and the city centre is more expensive than student housing.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It was extremely easy. The coordinator made sure that you were registered for the right courses. Email the coordinator if you experience some kind of trouble and it will be fixed for you.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: The coordinator sent a list of courses you could choose from. After a while, she sent out a survey from where I chose my courses from. I was not registered for one course that I had chosen in one instance, so a wrote her an email and she fixed it in no time.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The emailing with the coordinator.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Successful. There was no trouble for me.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There really is not much advice to give. Read your email from the coordinator and write her an email if you are in doubt or experience some kind of trouble.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Great courses. They only run for 7 weeks with exams in the 8th week and they are 4 ECTS. So if you want to take approximately 30 ECTS (32) you have to do four courses for each block. The curriculum is narrower and the courses are more niche than the courses at Economics at UCPH.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The courses are high-quality and the level is comparable to the level at UCPH. You will definitely feel a healthy challenge during the blocks and you will definitely feel like you have learned a lot after the exams. Since the courses are more niche you can dive deeper into parts of economics or finance that you otherwise wouldn't have been able to at UCPH.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: One lecture a week in every course and some had classes, but they weren't like the classes at UCPH. The classes were more focused on e.g. the lecturer refreshing some needed math for the course, Q&A's, review of tests etc. So more extra activities that they wouldn't waste time with in the normal lectures. Which is in contrast to UCPH where you use classes to review problem sets. The teaching at Erasmus relied more on you doing the work yourself, reading of more papers and less class-instructor teaching.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
International Finance - 4 ECTS
Advanced Behavioural Finance - 4 ECTS
Financial Innovations and Institutions - 4 ECTS
 Fixed Income Securities and Portfolio Management - 4 ECTS
Economics of Innovation - 4 ECTS
Industrial Organisation - 4 ECTS
Advanced Money, Credit and Banking - 4 ECTS
Advanced International Trade - 4 ECTS

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I mostly enjoyed the finance courses in the second block: "International Finance", "Advanced Behavioural Finance", "Financial Innovations and Institutions" and "Fixed Income Securities and Portfolio Management". I would recommend them all as they all have their own niche focus on different parts of finance. I enjoyed the structure and content of "Financial Innovations and Institutions" as you started by theory of different financial risks and then moved on to explaining how financial regulation continuously developed due to the types of risks and how banks changed their operations as a response to the regulations. This pattern followed and the course ended with examining the banks during COVID and whether regulations in the past decades made banks more robust to the pandemic when it hit in March. "Advanced Behavioural Finance" is also a nice course that looks at empirical evidence for deviations from standard financial theory. It is mainly structured around papers, their conclusions and how they are related to behavioural biases that deviate from financial theory.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: It wasn't an unexpected cost, but get a bike. The infrastructure is fantastic and it is the easiest way to move around in the city although public transport such as the tram is well-functioning as well. Regarding the bike I recommend Swapfiets.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: The prices are comparable to Danish prices. Groceries such as vegetables are marginally cheaper, but bars and restaurants are equally expensive.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: There is a great international community arranging all sorts of events. The main organizers is the student organzation Erasmus Student Network, ESN, arranging parties, trips within the Netherlands and to neighbouring countries, film screenings, introduction days

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
A lot of people enjoyed the Erasmus Sport membership which allowed you to use the numerous amount of facilities. For example, they have a huge ice skating arena that people enjoy and many people also enjoy playing Padel Tennis or Squash. If you enjoy sports there are almost no sports you cannot exercise in Rotterdam.

Social activities include trips, parties, art walks around the city and film screenings. However, all these are arranged by the student organization ESN rather than the university.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Travel around in the Netherlands. Rotterdam is very different from the rest of the Netherlands, but it is easy to travel around the country and I really recommend it. Moreover, Antwerpen in Belgium is just a short train ride away and if you are up for it there is a train from Rotterdam that takes you to Paris in 3 hours if want a weekend trip with new friends.

Experiencing the Dutch Bar life is always a recommendation and biking around the city.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Go for a run around Kralingse Bos. It is a nice, scenic route for your run. Other than that I recommend biking to neighbouring cities such as Delft and Gouda, which are smaller, nice, and more Dutch-styled cities. 

I also went to several football matches e.g. I saw the national team play in De Kuip in Rotterdam and I can definitely recommend it.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Easy. Dutch and Danish people get a long well and share many similarities with respect to their cultures, life-style and personalities (broadly speaking).

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Dutch people are known to be direct, so be direct with them. However, you will most likely spend more time with other internationals. Like in Denmark where Danes usually spend time with Danes unless they are on an international programme, Dutch also tend to socialize with other Dutch.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: None. I am pretty used to Dutch culture and Dutch people.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Dutch bar life with their special beers and a broad range of snacks such as bitterballen. Other than that you experience a large degree of openness and kindness and you get why people talk about Rotterdam as a young and vibrant city.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1) Grants or at least savings - Don't let your activities be determined by the need to save money. If you apply in advance you have a great opportunity to receive 25.000+ DKK that you can use down here and enhance your stay.
2) Raincoat - The weather is like Danish weather and you never know when it is going to rain or when the rain is going to stop.
3) Headphones - For when you're studying at the library on campus or at a café

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Get a bike.
Use libraries and cafés for studying if you like it as much as I do.
Go for a run around Kralingse Bos - My local route everytime.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Living in another country and make it your home for a semester and get a feeling of being connected to the city afterwards. Meeting people from different countries within and outside Europe. The academic level was rewarding as well. In the end many factors contributed to the exchange being a unique experience that gave me new perspectives.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: I had to get used to courses being shorter, so you had to focus from the beginning and couldn't fall too far behind. On the other hand, this teaches you to be more structured. While many say the workload is heavy, I disagree. Just make sure to study continuously rather than skipping here and there. Most of the curriculum will be present in the exam, so you can't gamble with what you read and what you don't.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
